prompt: Write an essay titled “A New Kind of Chemistry”. It explains how nuclear reactions, which rearrange the inside of the atom, differ from ordinary chemical reactions, and traces how people learned to use them. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
Chemistry, as chemists have practiced it for two centuries, is a science of rearrangement at the surface of the atom. When hydrogen burns in oxygen, or iron rusts, or sugar ferments, the nuclei stay exactly where they were. Only the outermost electrons move, forming and breaking bonds. Each atom keeps its identity, and the energy involved is small: burning one carbon atom releases about four electron volts, enough to lift a speck of dust a fraction of a nanometer. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen can be combined and recombined indefinitely, but they never turn into one another.

Nuclear reactions work at a different depth. They rearrange the nucleus, the dense core of protons and neutrons that holds nearly all of an atom's mass. When the nucleus changes its number of protons, the atom becomes a different element. When it sheds energy, the energy comes from the nucleus itself, and it is enormous by chemical standards. The binding energy that holds a nucleus together is roughly a million times greater than the energy binding electrons to atoms. A single uranium-235 fission event releases about 200 million electron volts, tens of millions of times more than the chemical energy in a carbon atom's combustion. Einstein's relation E = mc² explains the scale: a small fraction of the mass of the nucleus, converted to energy, is a great deal of energy.

People first encountered nuclear change without understanding it. In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts darkened photographic plates even in the dark, and Marie and Pierre Curie soon identified other radioactive substances. Radioactivity seemed to be a strange, spontaneous glow. Then, in the early 1900s, Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy showed that radioactive decay transforms one element into another. Radium becomes radon, and uranium eventually becomes lead. Soddy's conclusion was blunt: the alchemists had been pursuing something real, though they had lacked the means to achieve it.

The first deliberate transmutation came in 1919. Rutherford bombarded nitrogen gas with alpha particles, helium nuclei emitted by radioactive sources, and detected protons and oxygen. He had turned nitrogen into oxygen, and he had done it by striking the nucleus directly. The method was crude. Most alpha particles passed by without effect, and the yield was tiny. But it proved that the nucleus could be reached and reshaped.

Progress accelerated once physicists could build better projectiles. James Chadwick identified the neutron in 1932, a particle with no electric charge that could slip into nuclei without being repelled. Neutrons became the preferred tool. That same year, John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton split lithium nuclei using protons accelerated through high voltage, the first artificial nuclear reaction driven by a particle accelerator. Enrico Fermi, in Rome, then discovered that slowing neutrons with water or paraffin made them far more likely to be captured by nuclei, producing new radioactive isotopes. He and his colleagues made dozens of them.

The decisive surprise came in Berlin in December 1938. Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann bombarded uranium with neutrons and found barium, an element roughly half the mass of uranium, among the products. Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch, working in exile in Sweden, realized that the uranium nucleus had split in two, releasing a large amount of energy. They named the process fission. Within months, physicists confirmed that fission also released additional neutrons. That observation made a chain reaction conceivable: each fission could trigger further fissions.

In December 1942, beneath the stands of an unused squash court at the University of Chicago, Fermi's team built Chicago Pile-1, a stack of graphite and uranium that sustained a controlled chain reaction. The age of nuclear engineering had begun. Within three years the Manhattan Project had produced the first atomic bombs, and reactors at Hanford, Washington, were manufacturing plutonium, an element that Glenn Seaborg and colleagues had first made in 1940 and that does not occur naturally in useful quantities.

The same knowledge spread into peaceful uses. In 1954 the Soviet reactor at Obninsk became the first to supply electricity to a power grid. Radioisotopes became essential tools in medicine, industry, and science. Cobalt-60 sterilizes equipment and treats tumors, and technetium-99m is used in diagnostic imaging. Willard Libby's carbon-14 dating, developed around 1949, relies on a naturally occurring nuclear process to date ancient organic remains.

Nuclear chemistry, then, is not a separate branch of chemistry so much as a different regime of the same matter. Ordinary chemistry asks how atoms share and exchange electrons. Nuclear science asks what happens when the core itself is struck, split, or allowed to decay. Its discoveries have given humanity energy, medicine, and a new understanding of time, along with the capacity for catastrophe. The rules that govern this kind of chemistry were written only a century ago, and we are still learning how to use them well.
